2026 SEMA Show • Hybrid Honda Passport Throws More HP in Baja Racing Than Any Other 9.0-Liter V8-Powered Trophy Truck
Supreme Lamborghini Gallardo Restomod by Giugiaro Costs a Million Bucks, Donor Car Not Included
28 photos
Photo: GFG Projetti
Did the automotive world genuinely need a restomodded Lamborghini Gallardo in 2026, exactly 28 years after Fabrizio Giugiaro first sketched its razor-sharp wedge silhouette in 1998? Purists might argue that tampering with Sant'Agata Bolognese's ultimate volume-seller is borderline heresy, a cynical exercise in nostalgia aimed at deep-pocketed collectors chasing carbon-fiber vanity.
Yet, when the original architect himself picks up the pencil again, the conversation immediately shifts from sacrilege to redemption.
Unshackled from turn-of-the-millennium corporate bean-counters and industrial manufacturing compromises, Giugiaro decided his mid-engine creation deserved a ferocious upcycle. That explosive ambition materialized at the Concours at Wynn Las Vegas, where Giugiaro's Moncalieri-based GFG Style and CAVËN Atelier unveiled the Hommage 26.
Arriving seven days after the hand-beaten copper Peralta D coupé in Mexico and months after the Bizzarrini 5300 Aperta Lusso, the bright orange Lambo lookalike inaugurates CAVËN Atelier's Designer Series.
The official press release’s deliberate omission of the name of the vehicle that sired this Hommage a clever way to avoid trademark friction. However, the photographs leave zero doubt that the first-generation Lamborghini Gallardo stands at the foundation of this machine. Its cab-forward stance, steeply raked windshield, roofline arc, and compact mid-ship proportions are unmistakable signatures of Giugiaro's 1998 Italdesign proposal.
Photo: GFG Projetti While retaining those foundational bones, GFG Style replaced every single exterior panel with bespoke carbon-fiber bodywork, pulling the surfaces tighter and carving much more aggressive creases. Dressed in blazing orange with a contrasting black greenhouse, the nose preserves the vertical headlamp architecture of the original car. Critics immediately mocked it for the running mascara face, but that’s up to personal taste, so it’s beyond objective argumentation.
Crucially, the Hommage 26 finally realizes Giugiaro's 1998 vision of linking the headlights and gaping lower intakes through a concealed dual-bar horizontal LED lighting system. In profile, the supercar crouches over bespoke 20-inch five-spoke alloy wheels that frame an upgraded braking system, while deeply sculpted rockers feed reprofiled side cooling ducts.
Overhead, the black roof flows continuously into a louvered engine bay cover, culminating in an integrated rear spoiler flanked by two active aerodynamic side flaps. Giugiaro also engineered a new opening rear cabin window specifically to funnel raw exhaust acoustics directly inside the cockpit.
Photo: GFG Projetti The rear view represents the boldest visual departure from the donor supercar. A full-width black mesh fascia houses vertical twin-slat LED taillights paired with horizontal light blades, sitting above a sculpted diffuser and two wide rectangular tailpipes flanking the custom license plate.
Inside the cockpit, the overhaul continues with fresh instrument graphics and completely redesigned seats built to increase both lateral comfort and driving ergonomics.
Beneath the slatted decklid beats the naturally aspirated 5.0-liter V10 engine, thoroughly reworked by the wizards at Italtecnica to scream all the way to an 8,500 rpm redline. Buyers can specify the ten-cylinder powerhouse in a GT configuration producing 540 PS (533 hp) or a flagship Performance specification delivering 560 PS (552 hp). Power hits the tarmac exclusively through a traditional gated manual gearbox. Yes, 6-speed.
Photo: GFG Projetti To harness that high-revving fury, GFG Style equipped the chassis with a new electronically controlled suspension featuring selectable Comfort and Sport damping modes. Production is capped at 25 numbered examples worldwide, and you can’t simply walk into a showroom and place and order for it. you either bring a Gallardo along to be transmuted into a Hommage 26, or you designate CAVËN Atelier to source one.
Sounds easy, right? Well, the upcycling of a 2000s Lamborghini will set you back a cool €900,000. That’s a million bucks (and small change) at the November 1, 2026 exchange rate. That’s a fully loaded Revuelto SV (Super Veloce) with Ad Personam goodies bolted onto it. And it doesn't account for the extra $150K needed for the Gallardo donor car. Talk about restomods throwing the bank account under the bus.
Photo: GFG Projetti Compared to the stock first-generation Gallardo, the Hommage 26 sheds weight via carbon-fiber construction, introduces active rear aerodynamics, sharpens handling, and extracts up to 60 PS (59 hp) more from the 5.0-liter block.
Manufactured in Sant'Agata Bolognese from 2003 to 2013, the Lamborghini Gallardo amassed 14,022 units across a 10-year run, cementing its status as the brand's first production V10 and best-selling supercar of its era. Its expansive lineup included the Coupé, Spyder, SE, Nera, Superleggera, rear-wheel-drive LP 550-2 Valentino Balboni, LP 560-4, LP 570-4 Superleggera, Super Trofeo Stradale, and Squadra Corse. Neat lineage, and a lot of shoes for the Hommage 26 to fill.
Across that decade, Lamborghini deployed two distinct naturally aspirated V10 powerplants. First-generation cars built from 2003 to 2008 carried an even-firing powerhouse rated between 500 PS (493 hp) and 530 PS (523 hp). The 2008 facelift introduced a direct-injected, odd-firing 5.2-liter (5,204 cc) V10 delivering between 550 PS (542 hp) and 570 PS (562 hp). Both generations offered a 6-speed Graziano manual gearbox or a 6-speed e-gear automated sequential transmission.
Photo: GFG Projetti In 2003, the base Gallardo Coupé packed 500 PS (493 hp) and 510 Nm (376 lb-ft), sprinting from 0 to 100 kph (62 mph) in 4.2 seconds toward a 309 kph (192 mph) top speed, all for only $165,900. Conversely, the flagship 2013 LP 570-4 Squadra Corse boasted 570 PS (562 hp) and 540 Nm (398 lb-ft), hitting 100 kph (62 mph) in 3.4 seconds, reaching 325 kph (202 mph), and starting at $259,100.
Notably, the exact even-firing 5.0-liter V10 with 88 mm (3.46 in) cylinder bore spacing utilized in the Hommage 26 remained exclusive to Sant'Agata Bolognese, powering only the 1995 Giugiaro-styled Calà concept and 2003 to 2008 Gallardo models. However, its redesigned 5.2-liter successor powered the Lamborghini Huracán, Audi R8, C6 Audi S6, D3 Audi S8, and Italdesign Zerouno, while inspiring the twin-turbocharged 5.0-liter V10 in the ferocious C6 Audi RS6.
So, its this Hommage 26 a grand finale, a majestic throwback to a masterpiece, or a tentative “teach an old dog new tricks” act? After all, a million bucks for a V10 from 25 years ago with new makeup isn’t likely to become the holy grail Lamborghini Gallardo “What If” fans would throw money at.
